Amicable

/AM-ih-kuh-buhl/ - the stress falls on AM · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Amicable means friendly and free of conflict, especially between parties who might have quarreled.

The two labs had raced each other for a decade, yet the merger talks stayed amicable from the first handshake to the last signature.

Worked Example

When the food truck's owners decided to go separate ways, regulars braced for drama. The breakup was thoroughly amicable instead: they divided the recipes over coffee, auctioned the truck, and still cater each other's family parties.

Amicable is not about personality — it describes relations and agreements, especially between parties who could easily have fought. People are amiable; settlements, splits, and rivalries are amicable when goodwill replaces the expected conflict.

How Amicable Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

peaceable

peaceable: describes a temperament that avoids fighting, not a settlement

cooperative

cooperative: willing to work together, without implying a healed rivalry

Antonyms

acrimonious

acrimonious: bitter and sharp-tempered — the classic word for an ugly split

feuding

feuding: locked in an ongoing quarrel

How Strong Is It? — civil → amicable → harmonious

civil vs. amicable

civil vs. amicable: Civil stops short of amicable — civil rivals manage bare politeness at the door, while an amicable pair genuinely wishes each other well.

harmonious vs. amicable

harmonious vs. amicable: Harmonious goes further than amicable — amicable parties have settled their differences, while harmonious ones work so smoothly together that differences barely arise.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — amic-

Root — amic-: friend (Latin amicus)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: able, worthy of

Put it together

Put it together: Amic- ('friend,' Latin amicus) + -able = able to remain friends. Latin amicabilis produced both this word and amiable, but English split the twins: amiable went to personalities, amicable to dealings — the settlement, split, or rivalry where friendship wins out over the expected fight.

Use the root in a new word: enemy

Use the root in a new word: enemy: Your enemy is literally your not-friend: Latin inimicus, from in- (not) + amicus (friend).

Word Choice

neutral / slightly formal

Amicable belongs to relations, not personalities: an amicable divorce, split, or settlement between parties who might have quarreled. For a warm person, use amiable or affable (both in this unit). A quick test: if you can put 'settlement' after it, amicable is your word.
